cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply-Side Policies
cards.back: Supply-side policies aim to increase the economy's productive capacity by improving the efficiency and quality of factors of production.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply-Side Policies
cards.back: Investment in education and training: improves human capital, increases productivity, reduces structural unemployment by giving workers transferable skills.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply-Side Policies
cards.back: Lower direct taxes and business taxes: increase incentives to work and invest, but may reduce government revenue.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply-Side Policies
cards.back: Privatisation and deregulation: introduces competition and profit incentives, improving efficiency — but natural monopolies may exploit consumers.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply-Side Policies
cards.back: Trade union reform: reducing union power can make labour markets more flexible, but may reduce worker protection and lead to lower wages.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating supply-side policies, use the LIT framework: Longevity (do effects last?), Implementation time (how long until results?), Trade-offs (who loses?). Supply-side policies are most important for long-term growth but slowest to take effect.
Increase productive capacity (AS) (e.g. Increase or decrease aggregate demand (AD))
Long-run (years to take effect) (e.g. Short to medium-run (months))
Low: increases AS, reducing price pressure (e.g. Higher: if AD exceeds AS, inflation rises)
Education, infrastructure, deregulation (e.g. Interest rate changes, tax cuts, spending increases)
T-levels, Freeports, broadband investment (e.g. Bank Rate changes, furlough, VAT adjustments)
Slow to implement, expensive upfront (e.g. May cause inflation or increase debt if misused)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Supply-side policies always benefit everyone because they increase productive capacity. Correct: While supply-side policies increase overall capacity, benefits are not evenly distributed: privatisation may lead to job losses and higher prices; lower business taxes may benefit owners rather than workers; trade union reform weakens worker protections.
